title: When should I start talking to kids about money?
content: ## **When to Talk to Kids About Money!** Here's a secret: you're already talking to your children about money—and so is the world. The difference is that much of the teaching many parents do isn't intentional, unlike the messages children receive from advertisers, marketers, and social media influencers. And they aren't the only ones talking to and teaching children about money. Family members, friends, neighbors, peers, teachers, and community leaders all play a role. While their intentions are often good, they may not be well versed in basic money principles or aligned with your family's values, goals, and priorities. That lack of intentionality is a serious problem. It leaves a child's financial education to chance and to influences that may not have their best interests at heart. Over time, it can shape habits, attitudes, and beliefs about money that undermine long-term financial well-being and limit future opportunities. Parents need to know this: research, experience, and results all point to the same conclusion, **you cannot start your child's financial education too early.** Research from the University of Cambridge found that many adult money habits are largely formed by age seven. What's especially important to understand is that these habits become deeply ingrained over time. They are shaped less by logic and careful decision-making than by feelings, attitudes, repeated behaviors, and influences from the world around us. As a result, they often guide financial choices long before children develop the ability to think critically about money or align their decisions with their values, goals, and long-term well-being. Take a moment to let that sink in. What it means is the years between ages three and seven represent a critical window of opportunity to set your child on a path toward lifelong financial well-being, confidence, security, and opportunity. So start today. Begin addressing the challenge and helping children build a foundation for financial freedom, security, and opportunity by intentionally talking to them about—and teaching them—the most basic and fundamental money habits: (1) Learning to save and delay gratification. (2) Developing a strong work ethic and understanding the value of earning. (3) Spending smart—living on less than you earn. (4) Giving wisely and helping others. (5) Setting meaningful goals for your money. (6) Planning and tracking your money (budgeting). (7) Learning to invest and grow your money, including understanding the power of compound interest. These simple habits, practiced consistently over time, can profoundly shape a child's future and put them on a path toward greater confidence, independence, and financial well-being. **Grow Good Daily** At Grow Good Daily, we believe that intentional tiny steps—habits—rooted in time-tested principles and practiced consistently, lead to larger-than-expected results over time. By age three, children already understand the basic idea that things cost money. They've watched you tap a card, pull out a wallet, pay bills, or say, "We can't afford that right now." They're absorbing your relationship with money whether you're teaching them or not. The question isn't whether your children will learn about money from you. The question is: What will they learn? *The Grow Good Daily Principle* Young children do not need to understand interest rates, stock markets, or investment portfolios. They do need to understand that money is a tool—something you earn, save, spend wisely, and use thoughtfully to achieve goals and help others. Those values take root early. Financial education doesn't need to be a formal lesson. It can be woven into everyday moments at home, in the grocery store, at the gas pump, during family outings, on birthdays, and around the dinner table. **What Parents Can Do** Many parents avoid talking about money because they feel their own finances aren't perfect or because they weren't taught about money growing up. We hear this all the time at Grow Good Daily. But here's what we've learned: You don't need to be a financial expert to raise a financially confident child. You simply need to be intentional, honest, and present. *Narrate your decisions.* Let your children hear your thinking: Let your children hear your thinking: "I'm choosing the store brand because it's just as good and saves us money for our vacation fund." *Include children in age-appropriate decisions.* When appropriate, let them observe or participate in real-life money choices that reflect your family's values and priorities. *Normalize money conversations.* Talk about money the same way you talk about health, kindness, responsibility, or hard work. *Celebrate saving, not just spending.* Make deposits into a piggy bank, savings jar, or savings account a source of pride and accomplishment. *Treat mistakes as learning opportunities. * A child who spends all of their money too quickly isn't failing—they're learning. As we like to say: "The goal isn't to raise a child who never makes financial mistakes. The goal is to raise a child who has the language, values, confidence, and resilience to learn from them." **Why Starting Early Matters** When money education is delayed—or never happens intentionally—children fill the gap with what they observe and absorb from the world around them. That includes social media, peers, influencers, advertising, entertainment, and popular culture. The messages they receive are rarely neutral. Many are designed to equate spending with happiness, status, success, and belonging. Young adults who never learned to save, budget, delay gratification, or distinguish needs from wants don't suddenly develop those skills at age 18 or 22. Too often, they struggle with debt, impulse spending, financial stress, and anxiety about money that can persist for years. **A Final Thought** Financial literacy is not a subject. It's a lifelong practice. Families who practice it together—openly, consistently, and without shame—raise children who are better prepared for the opportunities and challenges of life. At Grow Good Daily, we believe small daily conversations create lasting roots. Money is one of the most powerful tools your child will ever have. Help them understand it. Help them respect it. Help them use it wisely. Start now—wherever your child is and wherever you are. Because the best time to start was yesterday.
